newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Private capital needed for Asia's power drive.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Private capital needed for Asia's power drive.

text.p: The staggering capital requirements for US$100 billion a year in developing Asian economies for new power generation plants could be met only five to 10 percent by multilateral development banks, a senior official of the Asian Development Bank said on Wednesday.

Vladimir Bohun, deputy director of the ADB's infrastructure, energy and financial sectors department, told a coal seminar the balance would have to come in the form of bilateral aid, export credits, commercial loans, internal cash generation of public utilities, direct private investments and domestic savings.

Bohun's statement added a new dimension to a major theme which has run through the APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum) coal conference that private power operators and private capital will play a new and greatly expanded role in making Asia's largely coal-fired power boom happen.

Total installed power capacity in developing member countries (DMC) of the ADB more than doubled in the 1980s to 310 gigawatts (GW) in 1990, then increased further to 408 GW in 1994, with 56 percent of it coal-fired, he said. But developing Asian countries still faced severe power shortages, Bohun said.

CMCs (China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Thailand, Hong Kong, Singapore, Korea, Taiwan) planned to boost installed capacity to about 640 GW by year 2000, he said. "The capital requurements of these generating capacity additions, as well as the associated transmission and distribution system expansion, are staggering," he said.
"Together with the capital requirements in the hydrocarbon sector, they are estimated to exceed US$100 billion per annum," he said. Bohun said the ADB strongly encouraged co-financing.
To the end of 1995, co-financiers had contributed US$21.9 billion to ADB-assisted projects, with official multilateral and bilateral sources contributing a 69 percent, Bohun said.
But even with official aid, credits and private investment, capital requirements would not be met unless public utilities increased internal cash generation by raising tariffs, he said.

Current average electricity tariffs in typical DMCs ranged from about four U.S. cents per kilowatt hour in India to about 12 cents U.S. in the Philippines. "In many DMCs, significant tariff increases will be unavoidable in the future," he said.

The deputy director of the Manila-based ADB, Asia's equivalent of the World Bank, said coal, currently the source for about 54 percent of primary commercial energy supply in all DMCs combined, would continue to play a dominant role in Asia.
Over the next 15 years, its use worldwide was expected to grow at more than two percent a year, with growth in Asia expected to be three times stronger than in the developed world.
China and India would account for almost 60 percent of projected global increase in coal demand, he said.

By year 2010, China was expected to use about 2.1 billion tonnes of coal and India about 500 million tonnes a year for a combined share of almost 50 percent of total world coal consumption, he said. China presently consumes 1.3 billion tonnes a year from its proven reserves of 290 billion tonnes, while India produced 270 million tonnes in 1995, he said.

Bohun was speaking in a "clean coal" section of the conference, which concentrated on the greenhouse gas emission issue. The ADB was willing to finance coal-fired power plants only if they complied with environmental standards, he said.
John Paffenbarger, an electricity market specialist with the International Energy Agency, said pollution controls added 20-25 percent to the cost of producing electricity.

Ted Atwood, international programs manager of the U.S. Department of Energy, said world-wide power investment requirements between 1995 and year 2010 were $2.3 trillion, with $1.5 trillion of this in developing and transitional countries.
But investment targets were reachable, with power taking only eight percent of total private investment and with $20 trillion globally under professional funds management.
